seo.title: 27 Pictorial Mark Logos Explained
seo.description: 27 famous pictorial mark logos explained by a brand designer: animals, objects, nature and people, from the Twitter bird and the Penguin to Apple, Shell and the Jordan Jumpman.

intro:
A pictorial mark is a logo that is a picture of a real, recognizable thing: an apple, a bird, a shell, a camera. Apple, Twitter, Shell and Target all use one. A good pictorial mark can drop the name entirely, because people know the picture on sight.

Logo design quick course: this guide is part of my series on logo types. Read the others on combination marks, emblem logos, script logos, mascot logos, wordmark logos, lettermark logos, monogram logos and abstract logos, or start with the overview of all types of logos.

What is a pictorial mark?

A pictorial mark, also called a logo symbol or brand mark, is an icon drawn from the real world. You could name the object in one word: bird, penguin, apple, eye, flame. Some brands use the picture alone, like Apple and Target. Others pair it with the name in a combination mark, like Nestlé or Allstate, and the picture still does most of the remembering.

Pictorial mark vs abstract mark vs mascot

These three symbol logos are easy to mix up. A pictorial mark shows a real thing, like the Apple apple. An abstract mark is a shape with no literal meaning, like the Nike Swoosh or the Mastercard circles. A mascot is a character with a personality, like Colonel Sanders or the Duolingo owl. The Twitter bird is a pictorial mark because it is just a bird; Duo the owl is a mascot because he has a face, a name and a voice.

When the name is the picture

The strongest pictorial marks show exactly what the name says. Apple is an apple, Shell is a shell, Target is a target, Penguin is a penguin and Dove is a dove. People hear the name and see the picture, or see the picture and remember the name. That loop is why these brands can drop the words.

When the name is not a thing, the picture can tell a story instead: Evernote's elephant never forgets, Red Bull's charging bulls are a picture of energy and Allstate's cupped hands are its slogan, "You're in good hands".

The two risks: clichés and growing out of the picture

Clichés. Light bulbs for ideas, globes for global companies, leaves for anything green: these pictures are so common that they make a brand look like everyone else. A pictorial mark only works if your picture is yours, in your market.

Growing out of the picture. A literal picture can box a business in. Apple outgrew computers without trouble, because an apple says nothing about computers. A company called "Phone Shop" with a phone logo would struggle if it started selling laptops. And a picture can be thrown away by a new owner: Twitter's famous bird was replaced by the X in 2023.

Why pictorial marks keep getting simpler

Almost every pictorial mark in this list has lost detail over the years. Shell's scallop went from a realistic shell to Raymond Loewy's clean outline in 1971, Instagram swapped its retro camera for a flat outline in 2016, Mozilla simplified the Firefox fox in 2019 and Peugeot reduced its full lion to a head in a shield in 2021. The reason is screens: a picture now has to read as a 16-pixel favicon and an app icon, not only on a sign.

Below are 27 famous pictorial marks in three groups of nine: animals, objects, and nature and people. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation.

logoResearch.name: Twitter
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Martin Grasser drew the Twitter bird in 2012 from overlapping circles, and it was replaced by the X in July 2023.
observations: A blue bird with its head tilted up, mid-song.
Built only from arcs of circles, it stays smooth at any size.

logoResearch.name: Penguin Books
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Edward Young sketched the Penguin at London Zoo in 1935, and Pentagram's Angus Hyland redrew it in 2003.
observations: A black and white penguin stands inside an orange oval.
The bird says the books are cheerful and cheap, not stuffy.

logoResearch.name: Peugeot
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Peugeot has used a lion since 1850, first to mark its steel saw blades, and unveiled a lion's head in a shield in 2021.
observations: A lion's head with a flowing mane sits inside a black shield.
The lion stood for the strength and sharpness of the saw blades.

logoResearch.name: Red Bull
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dietrich Mateschitz launched Red Bull in Austria in 1987, based on the Thai drink Krating Daeng, which means red gaur.
observations: Two red bulls charge at each other in front of a yellow sun.
The clash of the bulls is a picture of energy.

logoResearch.name: Evernote
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Evernote chose an elephant because an elephant never forgets, which is what a note app promises.
observations: A green elephant's head with a curled trunk.
The folded ear doubles as the turned corner of a page.

logoResearch.name: Dove
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lever Brothers launched Dove soap in the United States in 1957.
observations: A small golden dove flies under a flowing script wordmark.
The dove suggests softness and calm, which suits a beauty soap.

logoResearch.name: Lufthansa
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Otto Firle drew the Lufthansa crane in 1918 for Deutsche Luft-Reederei, and it was redrawn in dark blue in 2018.
observations: A flying crane sits inside a thin circle next to the name.
A bird in flight is the most literal symbol an airline can have.

logoResearch.name: Nestlé
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Nestlé nest comes from Henri Nestlé's family crest, because Nestle means little nest in his Swabian dialect.
observations: A mother bird feeds two chicks in a nest above the name.
In 1988 the three chicks became two and the name moved under the nest.

logoResearch.name: Firefox
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jon Hicks drew the fox curled around a globe in 2004, and Mozilla simplified it in 2019.
observations: An orange fox wraps its body around a purple globe.
The fox's tail becomes a flame, a nod to the fire in the name.

logoResearch.name: Instagram
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Instagram replaced its retro camera icon with a flat camera outline on a colour gradient in 2016.
observations: A rounded camera outline sits on a purple, pink and orange gradient.
The gradient is a memory of the rainbow stripe on the old camera icon.

logoResearch.name: WhatsApp
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jan Koum and Brian Acton founded WhatsApp in 2009.
observations: A phone handset sits inside a green speech bubble.
Phone plus speech bubble: calls and chats in one picture.

logoResearch.name: YouTube
logoResearch.verifiedFact: YouTube was founded in 2005, and its red play button became the main symbol in 2017.
observations: A white play triangle sits in a red rounded rectangle.
The rectangle is an old TV screen, the triangle is the play button.

logoResearch.name: Dropbox
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dropbox flattened its open-box symbol in a 2017 rebrand.
observations: Four blue diamonds form an open box, seen from above.
The box is drawn in isometric view, a nod to the 3D icon it replaced.

logoResearch.name: Target
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Target opened its first store in Roseville, Minnesota, in 1962 with the bullseye as its logo.
observations: A red dot inside a red ring on white.
The name and the picture are the same thing, so the logo needs no words.

logoResearch.name: Windows
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Windows 11 logo of 2021 shows four equal blue panes, a window seen straight on.
observations: Four blue squares with thin gaps form a window.
Earlier versions waved like a flag; the new one is just a window.

logoResearch.name: Telegram
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pavel and Nikolai Durov launched Telegram in 2013.
observations: A white paper plane flies inside a blue circle.
A paper plane is the oldest way to send a message across a room.

logoResearch.name: Hermès
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Hermès carriage comes from a painting by Alfred de Dreux and has been the house logo since the 1940s.
observations: A horse-drawn carriage with a groom waiting sits above the name.
Hermès began as a harness maker in 1837, so the carriage tells its story.

logoResearch.name: Google Maps
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Google gave Maps its new pin icon in 2020, for the app's 15th birthday.
observations: A map pin filled with Google's four colours.
The pin shape alone says location, in any language.

logoResearch.name: Apple
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rob Janoff designed the Apple logo in 1977, and it lost its rainbow stripes in 1998.
observations: A black apple with a bite out of the right side and a leaf on top.
The bite makes it an apple at a glance, not a cherry or a tomato.

logoResearch.name: Shell
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Shell has used a scallop shell since 1904, and Raymond Loewy drew the current version in 1971.
observations: A yellow scallop shell with a red outline.
The name started with Marcus Samuel's father, who sold seashells in London.

logoResearch.name: Prudential
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Prudential has used the Rock of Gibraltar as its symbol since 1896.
observations: A blue rock rises from the sea next to the name.
A rock is the strongest picture of safety an insurer could choose.

logoResearch.name: Air Canada
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Air Canada brought back a red maple leaf on black and white in its 2017 rebrand.
observations: A red maple leaf inside a red ring next to the name.
The national symbol turns the airline into the country's flag carrier.

logoResearch.name: Tinder
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tinder launched in 2012, and its flame plays on the name: tinder is what you use to start a fire.
observations: A red flame with a curl at the base.
One simple shape that works as a tiny app icon.

logoResearch.name: CBS
logoResearch.verifiedFact: William Golden designed the CBS eye in 1951.
observations: A black pupil inside an eye shape inside a circle.
An eye is the perfect symbol for a TV network: it watches and is watched.

logoResearch.name: Allstate
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Allstate's 'good hands' slogan dates from 1950, and the cupped hands became its logo.
observations: Two cupped blue hands sit in a circle next to the name.
The picture is the slogan: you're in good hands.

logoResearch.name: Jordan
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Jumpman silhouette of Michael Jordan first appeared on the Air Jordan III in 1988.
observations: A black silhouette of a player leaping with the ball held high.
No name needed: the pose itself is the brand.

logoResearch.name: NBA
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Alan Siegel designed the NBA logo in 1969, based on a photo of Jerry West.
observations: A white player silhouette dribbles between red and blue.
Red, white and blue tie the league to America.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 pictorial marks in one consistent format, grouped into animals, objects, and nature and people.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size or success of the company behind it.
sectionIntroductions: Animals are the most common pictures in logos, because each one carries a ready-made meaning: a lion is strong, a dove is gentle, an elephant never forgets.
Everyday objects make some of the clearest logos: a camera, a phone, a play button, a paper plane. Everyone knows what they do.
Fruit, shells, rocks, flames and people: pictures from nature and the human body that brands have made their own.
sectionBridge: This is a visual study of pictorial marks, not a ranking of companies.
Look at how much detail each picture keeps, and whether you would recognize it without the name.
entryFallbacks: The picture is simple enough to recognize at a glance.
Notice how it would read as a small app icon.

findings.heading: The name and the picture match
findings.text: Apple, Shell, Target, Penguin and Dove show exactly what their names say, so the two remind people of each other.

findings.heading: One twist makes it yours
findings.text: The bite in the apple, the fox's flame tail and the elephant's page-corner ear turn a common picture into a unique one.

findings.heading: Pictures keep getting simpler
findings.text: Shell, Instagram, Firefox and Peugeot all removed detail so their symbols work as app icons.

findings.heading: A picture crosses languages
findings.text: A bird, an eye or a maple leaf needs no translation, which helps global brands like Lufthansa and Air Canada.

findings.heading: Owners can throw them away
findings.text: Twitter's bird, one of the best-known pictures online, was replaced by the X in 2023.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a pictorial mark
checklistItems: Can you name the object in one word?
Does it say something true about the brand?
Does it have one twist no competitor has?
Does it read at 16 pixels and in one colour?
Will it still fit if the business grows into new products?
logoRosterConfig.conclusionHtml:
How to design a pictorial mark

1. Pick one object. Choose a single thing that says something true about the brand: its name, its origin or its promise. One object, not a scene.

2. Draw it simply. Reduce the object to a few bold shapes. Remove details until it starts to look like something else, then put the last one back.

3. Make it yours. Add one twist no one else has: the bite in the Apple apple, the folded ear on the Evernote elephant, the flame tail on the Firefox fox. Without a twist, it is clip art.

4. Test it small. Check the picture at 16 pixels, in one colour and next to competitors. If it turns into a blob or looks like a rival, simplify it again.

Want a picture people remember?

A great pictorial mark shows one real thing, drawn simply, with a twist that makes it yours. When the name and the picture match, the logo can eventually stand on its own, the way Apple, Shell and Target do.

faq.question: What is a pictorial mark?
faq.answer: A pictorial mark is a logo that shows a picture of a real, recognizable thing, like the Apple apple, the Twitter bird, the Shell shell or the Target bullseye. It can be used alone or next to the brand name.

faq.question: What is the difference between a pictorial mark and an abstract mark?
faq.answer: A pictorial mark shows something real, like an apple or a bird. An abstract mark is a shape with no literal meaning, like the Nike Swoosh or the Mastercard circles.

faq.question: What is the difference between a pictorial mark and a mascot?
faq.answer: A pictorial mark is a picture of a thing. A mascot is a character with a personality, a face and often a name, like Colonel Sanders or the Duolingo owl.

faq.question: Is a pictorial mark good for a new business?
faq.answer: It can be, especially when the name is a real thing. Most new businesses should pair the picture with the name at first, in a combination mark, and let the picture stand alone once people know it.

faq.question: How much does a pictorial mark logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices vary a lot by designer. I design a complete brand identity, including the logo symbol and all its versions, in one week for a flat $3,000.
